```{=latex}
{\tiny \textit{The following analysis uses Whanganui Council rates from 2022 to 2026 only. Total rates are analyses, these are comprised of fixed and variable portions. For the purpose of this analysis separating the fixed and variable portions was not necessary as the component breakdown per council service was not the subject.}}
```

```{r library setup, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
library(tidygraph)
library(tidyverse)
library(readxl)
library(ggdist)
library(maps)    
library(sf)  
library(patchwork)
library(igraph)
library(ggraph)
library(showtext)
font_add_google("Inter", "Inter")
showtext_auto()
```

```{r data setup, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
#===== Read in data ======#
# Unit_Rates <- read_excel("Draft Rates by property 26.27 - statistical purposes 1.xlsx", sheet = "Unit Rates")
wdc_rates <- read_csv("wdc_rates_qv.csv") %>% 
  mutate(rate_yr = factor(rate_yr, levels = c("22_23", "23_24", "24_25", "25_26", "26_27"), ordered = TRUE))

#===== map setup begin ======#
nz <- read_sf("nz_sa3.gpkg")
#read_sf("https://www.massey.ac.nz/~jcmarsha/data/nz_map/sa3_data.sqlite")

ta_nz <- nz %>% 
  group_by(territorial_authority, regional_council) %>%
  summarise(geometry = st_union(geom), .groups = 'drop')

whanganui <- nz %>% filter(territorial_authority == "Whanganui District") %>%
  mutate(sa3_name = recode(sa3_name,
                           "Otamatea (Whanganui District)" = "Otamatea",
                           "Whanganui District Rural" = "Rural",
                           "Bastia-Durie Hill-Putiki" = "Bastia-Durie"))

bbox <- st_bbox(whanganui)

w_bbox <- list(x = c(1767500, 1779000), y=c(5574000, 5585000))
#===== map setup finish ======#

#===== Mapping Suburbs begin =====#
St_John_Streets <- c('Acton Pl', 'Aiken Rd', 'Alexa Pl', "Brassey Rd","Bristow St", "Chittick Pl","Collier Pl", "Dickson Cres", "Halswell St","Halswell Street","Hillside Tce", "Kent Rd","Linda Pl", "Ngapuhi St", "Oakland Ave","Parkes Ave", "Parsons St", "Porritt St", "Rawhiti Pl", "Smart Tce", "St Leonard St","Taranaki St","Tarata St", "Tregarth St","Tulloch St", "Virginia Rd", 'Peakes Rd', 'Victoria Park', 'Virginia Lake (Rotokawau)')

Otamatea_Streets <- c('Sewerage Pump Turere', 'Babbage Pl', 'Beachcroft', "Chelsea Cl", "Cotswolds Cl", "Diana Pl", "Eaton Cres", "Edith Collier Dr", "Edmonds Dr", "Goldsbury Pl", "Gumtree Rise", "Holdsworth Dr", "Kawau Pl", "Lancewood Pl", "Lithgow Dr", "Mannington Rd", "Montgomery Rd", "Norfolk Dr", "Otamatea Reserve", "Perrett Dr", "Pickwick Rd", "Rotokawau Dr", "Sandcroft Dr", "Sandy Lane", "St Johns Hts", "Suffolk Dr", "Tasman Views", "Tirimoana Pl", "Turere Pl","Virginia Hts", "Webster Pl", "Pukeko Drive", 'Tangaroa View', 'Middens Way')

Springvale_streets <-c('Addenbrooke Tce')

Whanganui_Centre_Streets <- c('Pitt St', 'Peat Pl', 'Peat St')

#===== Mapping suburbs finish =====

#===== Data wrangling begin =====
streets <- wdc_rates %>% 
  filter(suburb == "St Johns/Otamatea") %>% 
  select(property_no, rate_yr, property_address, suburb) %>%
  mutate(
    house_num = as.integer(str_extract(property_address, "^\\s*(\\d+)")), 
    street = str_remove(property_address, "~.*"),
    street = str_remove(street, "-."),
    street = str_remove(street, "^(?i:unit\\s+)?(?:[\\d/][\\d/A-Za-z]*\\s+)+"), #handles numbers and numbers like 9A,alos UNIT 6C / 59 and
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    suburb = case_when(
      #house numbers on great north road. great north road spans both. Lower number in St Johns up to 117. Then 119 and 121 are St Johns. 118, 120 and 122 onwards are otamtea
      street == "Great North Rd" & is.na(house_num) ~ "St Johns Hill",
      street == "Great North Rd" & house_num <= 117 ~ "St Johns Hill",
      street == "Great North Rd" & house_num %in% c(119, 121) ~ "St Johns Hill",
      street == "Great North Rd" & house_num >= 118 ~ "Otamatea (Whanganui District)",
      #easier ones
      street %in% St_John_Streets ~ "St Johns Hill",
      street %in% Otamatea_Streets ~ "Otamatea (Whanganui District)",
      street %in% Springvale_streets ~ "Springvale",
      street %in% Whanganui_Centre_Streets ~ "Whanganui Centre",
      TRUE ~ suburb
    )
  ) %>% select(property_no, rate_yr, suburb) #for left join

#join tdatasets to get what I need. Remove nulls from data set.
Rates <- wdc_rates %>% 
  filter(!is.na(assessment_number)) %>%
  mutate( #mapping qv_category to res/com/farm for simpler groupings
    Category = case_when(
      `qv category` %in% c('Commercial', 'Industrial') ~ 'Commercial', 
      `qv category` %in% c('Farming', 'Dairy', 'Pastoral', 'Forestry', 'Horticulture', 'Mining') ~ 'Farming',
      `qv category` %in% c('Other', 'Specialist', 'Utility asset') ~ 'Specialist',
      `qv category` %in% c('Residential', 'Lifestyle') ~ 'Residential',
      TRUE ~ `qv category`)
    ) %>%
  left_join(streets, by = c('property_no', 'rate_yr'), suffix = c("", "_new")) %>%
  mutate(suburb = coalesce(suburb_new, suburb)) %>%
  mutate(
    suburb = recode(suburb,
    "Bastia/Durie Hills Putiki" = "Bastia-Durie Hill-Putiki",
    "Whanganui Central" = "Whanganui Centre",
    "Whanganui Rural" = "Whanganui District Rural",)
  ) %>%
  mutate(year = case_when(
    rate_yr == '22_23' ~ 2022,
    rate_yr == '23_24' ~ 2023,
    rate_yr == '24_25' ~ 2024,
    rate_yr == '25_26' ~ 2025,
    rate_yr == '26_27' ~ 2026,
    TRUE ~ NA,
    ),
    QV = cv + lv + (cv - lv),
    rate_per_m = `rate area (ha)` * 10000) %>%
  mutate(Category = factor(Category, 
                           levels = c('Specialist', 'Farming', 'Commercial', 'Residential'))) %>% #for consistent color coding
  select(-suburb_new) %>%
  mutate(suburb = recode(suburb, 
                         "Otamatea (Whanganui District)" = "Otamatea",
                         "Whanganui District Rural" = "Rural",
                         "Bastia-Durie Hill-Putiki" = "Bastia-Durie"))

#ranking for suburbs by median rates in 2026
Suburb_rank <- Rates %>%
  filter(Category == "Residential", year == 2026) %>%
  group_by(suburb) %>% 
  summarise(m = median(`total rates`)) %>%
  mutate(rank = rank(-m, ties.method = "min")) %>%   
  arrange(rank)    

Residential <- Rates %>%
  filter(Category == "Residential") %>%
  mutate(suburb = factor(suburb, levels = Suburb_rank$suburb))

#===== Data wrangling finish =====#
```

```{r theme setup}
#===== Colour palette setup =====#
whanganui_palette <- function(n = 13, which = NULL) {
  pal <- c( #from inspecting the page elements of the Whanganui website, then color dropper picking from the coat of arms
  "#2757A2", 
  "#FEC30E",
  "#AD1619",
  "#008242", 
  "#DCC0E2", 
  "#C7E9F3",
  "#687928",
  "#D4582A",
  "#8B514E",
  "#93735B",
  "#372502",
  "#004925",
  "#FEEAD7",
  "black")
  
  if (!is.null(which)) {
    pal[which]
  }
  else if (n <= length(pal)) {
    pal[seq_len(n)]
  } else {
    grDevices::colorRampPalette(pal)(n)
  }
}

#===== Custom theme =====#
# font is Inter sans-serif, from website inspect elements on Whanganui council
theme_report <- function(base_size = 10) {
  theme_minimal(base_size = base_size, base_family = "Inter") +
    theme(
      # Titles
      plot.title = element_text(size = 15, face = "bold", hjust = 0),
      plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 12, hjust = 0,
                                   margin = margin(b = 5)),
      # Axes
      axis.title = element_text(size = 10),
      axis.text = element_text(size = 8),
      # Facet strips
      strip.text = element_text(face = "bold", size = 10),
      # Legend
      legend.position = "top",
      legend.title = element_text(size = 10),
      legend.text = element_text(size = 8),
      # Caption
      plot.caption = element_text(size =8)
    )
}

theme_map <- function(base_size = 10) {
  theme_minimal(base_size = base_size, base_family = "Inter") +
    theme(
      # panels
      panel.grid.major = element_blank(),
      panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
      # Titles
      plot.title = element_text(size = 15, face = "bold", hjust = 0),
      plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 12, hjust = 0),
      # Axes
      axis.title =  element_blank(),
      axis.text =  element_blank(),
      # Legend
      legend.title = element_text(size = 10),
      legend.text = element_text(size = 8)
    )
}
```

```{r graph 1 - map}
#===== Map Graph function =====#
#this funcrtion remains from my work when I was testing different fill values
map_graph <- function(data, fill, title) {
data %>%
  ggplot() +
  geom_sf(mapping=aes(fill = .data[[fill]]), col = 'white', linewidth = 1, alpha = 0.5) +
  coord_sf(xlim = w_bbox$x, ylim = w_bbox$y) + #need to change the rural district label to be visible
  #annotation
  geom_sf_label(mapping = aes(label = paste0(sa3_name, "\nn= ",as.character(count))), 
               size = 2) + 
  annotate("label", x = 1777000, y = 5584000,
           label = paste0("Rural\nn=", rural_count), 
           size = 2, fill = 'white') + #play with this to get the position right
  #Scale arguments
  scale_fill_gradientn(colors = scales::alpha(whanganui_palette(3), 0.7),
                       limits = range(data[[fill]]),
                       name = paste0(title, " (Thousands)"),
                       labels = scales::label_number(scale = 1/1000)) +
  #Labels
  labs(title = "",
       subtitle = '',
       x = '',
       y = '') +
  #Theme
  theme_map() +
  theme(legend.position = c(0.0, 0.0),
        legend.justification = c(0, 0),
        legend.direction = "horizontal",
        legend.title.position = "top",
        text = element_text(family = "Inter", size = 5))
}

#===== Wrangling =====#
graph_3_data <- Rates %>% 
  filter(year == 2026, Category == 'Residential') %>%
  group_by(suburb) %>%
  summarise(median_rates = median(`total rates`),
            count = n(),
            total = sum(`total rates`),
            .groups = 'drop') 

map_data <- whanganui %>%
  left_join(graph_3_data, by = c('sa3_name' = "suburb")) 

#get count of units in suburb for labels
#this is separate because the labels wants to be out of the bounding box window
rural_count <- graph_3_data %>%
  filter(suburb == 'Rural') %>%
  pull(count)

#===== Median rates map =====#
median_map <- map_graph(map_data, "median_rates", 'Median rates')

```

```{r graph 2 - dot and box}
#===== wrangling =====#
Total_rates_suburb <- Residential %>%
  filter(year == 2026) %>%
  group_by(suburb) %>% 
  summarise(t = sum(`total rates`))

graph_2_data <- Residential %>%
  filter(year == 2026) %>% #avoid double counting
  left_join(Total_rates_suburb %>% select(suburb, t), by = "suburb") %>%
  mutate(suburb_label = factor(
    paste0(suburb, "\nTotal rates = $", round(t / 1e6, 1), "M"),
    levels = paste0(Suburb_rank$suburb, "\nTotal rates = $",
                    round(Total_rates_suburb$t[match(Suburb_rank$suburb,
                                                     Total_rates_suburb$suburb)] / 1e6, 1), "M")
  ))

max_row <- graph_2_data %>%
  filter(year == 2026) %>%
  slice_max(`total rates`, n = 1)

#final dataset
graph_2_data <- graph_2_data %>%
  filter(!(`total rates` == max_row$`total rates`))

#===== box and dots =====#
box_suburbs <- graph_2_data %>%
  mutate(suburb_label = forcats::fct_rev(as.factor(suburb_label))) %>% 
  ggplot(aes(x=log(`total rates`), y = suburb_label, col= suburb)) +
  geom_point(position = position_jitterdodge(jitter.width = 1), alpha = 0.3, size = 1, shape = 16) +
  geom_boxplot(col = 'black', fill = NA, outlier.shape = NA, size = 0.7) +
  #annotation specific code. The max rates unit
  geom_point(data = max_row,
             aes(x = log(`total rates`), y = suburb_label),
             colour = "#687928", size = 3, inherit.aes = FALSE) +
  annotate("point",
           x = log(max_row$`total rates`),
           y = max_row$suburb_label,
           size = 8, colour = "black", shape = 1) +
  #scales
  scale_color_manual(values = whanganui_palette()) +
  #labels
  labs(title = "",
    subtitle = "",
       y = '', 
       x = 'Log of total rates') +
  #theme
  theme_report() +
  theme(legend.position = 'none',
        panel.grid.major.y = element_blank())
```

Residential rate payers make up 88.4% of rateable units and 77% of total rate income. The majority of the rate burden falls on them. Which raises discussion around the size of the rates bill, who pays more and whether rates are 'fair'. For this analysis residential rates refers to both residential and lifestyle QV categories.

The answer to who pays the most residential rates is not a simple one. Otamatea rate payers pay the highest median rates in 2026 at \$5,213. As a group they paid only \$3 million. While the owner of property 4849 in Gonville paid the most rates individually. Rates are not evenly spread and nor are people. Suburbs like Otamatea have few residents, while ones like Gonville (with median rates of \$3,928) have many. More residents mean more chance for outliers, hence the box pot below shows the logarithm of the rates in order to show the distribution of rates within each suburb neatly. It is also interesting to note that suburb size does not directly lead to more rates, because housing density is not a factor of suburb size.

```{r graph 3 - proportion}
#==== Wrangling ====#
equal_prop <- Residential %>%
  group_by(year) %>%
  summarise(prop = 100 / n(), .groups = "drop") %>%
  tidyr::crossing(suburb = unique(Residential$suburb))

#prop data
graph_3_data <- Residential %>%
  group_by(year) %>%
  mutate(prop = 100 * `total rates` / sum(`total rates`)) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  group_by(year, suburb) %>%
  reframe(median_qi(prop, .width = c(.25, .50, .80, .95)))

#==== Graph ====#
proportion_graph <- graph_3_data %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = year, y = y)) +
  geom_lineribbon(aes(ymin = ymin, ymax = ymax),
                  color = "#DC0100", alpha = 0.5, linewidth = 0.7) +
  geom_line(data = equal_prop, aes(x = year, y = prop),
            col = "black", linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 0.7) +
  facet_wrap(~ suburb, ncol = 5) +
  #scale arguments
  scale_x_continuous(labels = function(x) x %% 100) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("#C7E9F3", "#92B8D8", "#5C88BD","#2757A2"),
                    name = "Quantiles") +
  #labels
  labs(title = "Rate payments are not evenly spread.",
       subtitle = "Otamatea rate payers pay proportionally the most rates",
       x = "Year",
       y = "Proportion of rates paid per unit",
       caption = "Black dotted line is the proportion if every house paid the same share towards rates.") +
  #theme
  theme_report()
```

So, if the answer to who pays the most isn't straight forward, can we at least understand if it is fair? Presumably, rates are fairly allocated because all rate payers pitch in for all the facilities.

This is not the case. Generally speaking, Otamatea and St Johns Hill pay proportionally more than other suburbs in rates (0.007 median per unit). If every suburb were even, then the median proportion (red line) would be near the black dotted line of a 'perfectly proportioned rate payment'. Medians are idealised, so we could say that we may expect the 25% or maybe even 50% quantiles to contain the black dotted line. This is the case for suburbs Springvale, Bastia-Durie, Whanganui East and Centre, Aramohoro and Gonville. While rural pays only a median of 0.004 per unit.

So rates are not evenly spread, nor have they been since 2022. Some people pay more for facilities than everyone else.

```{r graph 4 - area}
#===== Wrangling =====#
residential_area <- Residential %>% 
  filter(!is.na(`rate area (ha)`)) 

Rates_per_meter <- residential_area %>% 
  summarise(total_rates = sum(`total rates`), 
            total_area = sum(rate_per_m),
            rate_per_ha = total_rates / total_area) %>%
  pull()

suburb_area <- residential_area %>% 
  group_by(suburb) %>%
  summarise(median = round(median(rate_per_m), 0)) 

graph_4_data <- residential_area %>%
  mutate(rates_per_area = `total rates` / rate_per_m) %>%
  group_by(suburb, year) %>%
  reframe(median_qi(rates_per_area, .width = c(.25, .50, .80, .95))) %>%
  left_join(suburb_area %>% select(suburb, median), by = "suburb") %>%
  mutate(suburb_label = factor(
    paste0(suburb, "\nmedian area = ", median),
    levels = paste0(Suburb_rank$suburb, "\nmedian area = ", 
                    suburb_area$median[match(Suburb_rank$suburb, suburb_area$suburb)])
  ))

#===== Graph =====#
area_graph <- graph_4_data %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = year, y = y)) +
  geom_lineribbon(aes(ymin = ymin, ymax = ymax),
                  color = "#DC0100", alpha = 0.5, linewidth = 0.7) +
  geom_hline(aes(yintercept = Rates_per_meter), col = "black",
             linetype = 'dashed') +
  facet_wrap(~ suburb_label, ncol = 5) +  
  #scale arguments
  scale_x_continuous(labels = function(x) x %% 100) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::label_number(accuracy = 1)) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("#C7E9F3", "#92B8D8", "#5C88BD","#2757A2"),
                    name = "Quantiles") +
  #labels
  labs(title = "Rates are not obviosuly linked to area.",
       subtitle = "The largest areas pay the least per meter squared. ",
       x = "Year",
       y = "Rates per m² (NZD)",
       caption = "Black dotted line is the average rates per meter squared across all Whanganui.") +
  #themes
  theme_report() 
```

If rate payers are not evenly paying for rates, is there some reason that may account for it? Do rate payers who have larger properties pay more, and is that why? Again, no. If this were the case we'd expect that suburbs with larger median areas show higher median lines than other suburbs. Rural properties get the lowest rate cost per meter squared (\$0.31), below the average rates per meter squared. Only the 80% quantile and higher pay this and above. Most other suburbs pay a median of \$5 - \$6 per meter in rates, while Whanganui Centre pays a median of \$7 - \$8 per meter. However, there is significant overlap in the quantises across all suburbs. Clearly, land is not uniformly priced nor distributed across suburbs, which can be obscured in aggregate analyses like this one.

```{r graph 5 - QV network}
#===== Wrangling =====#
set.seed(21)

prop <- 1000 / nrow(Residential %>% filter(year == 2026))

street_data <- Residential %>% 
  filter(year == 2026) %>%
  select(property_no, assessment_number, property_address, suburb, QV, year, `total rates`) %>%
  mutate(
      street = str_remove(property_address, "~WHANGANUI.*$"),
      street = str_remove(street, "^\\s*\\d+\\s*"),
      assess_num = str_remove(assessment_number, "[A-Z]+$") |> as.numeric()
  ) %>%
  filter(!is.na(street)) %>%
  group_by(suburb) %>%
  slice_sample(prop = prop) %>%
  ungroup() 

# Build edges using assessment_no as the ID. It it a proxy for closeness that is easier to work with. I looked through the data and that is what I saw. Streets were alphabetically arranged, by street number within suburbs with the property number indicating closeness. 
street_edges <- street_data %>%
  select(property_address, suburb, street, QV, assess_num) %>%
  rename(from = QV, from_id = assess_num) %>%
  left_join(
    street_data %>%
      select(property_address, suburb, street, QV, assess_num) %>%
      rename(to = QV, to_id = assess_num),
    by = c("suburb", "street"),
    relationship = "many-to-many"
  ) %>%
  filter(
    from_id != to_id,
    #set the number of neighbours used... assessment ids are proxy for neighbouring units, so larger mean more nieghbours, smaller value here means fewer. 
    abs(from_id - to_id) <= 1000000000, #10 digits is max
    from_id < to_id
  ) %>%
  #price of point of origin, to the nearby units, normalised so 1 = the same QV, and 0 = most different. 
  mutate(sim = 1 - abs(from - to) / max(from, to)) %>%
  #toggle similarity level. 
  filter(sim >= 0.5) %>%
  select(from_id, to_id, sim, suburb)

# Build graph — vertices are property_no (unique)
g <- graph_from_data_frame(
  street_edges %>% select(from_id, to_id, sim, suburb),
  vertices = street_data %>%
    distinct(assess_num, suburb) %>%
    set_names(c("name", "suburb")),
  directed = FALSE
)

#===== Plot =====#
QV_cluster <- ggraph(g, layout = "fr") +
  geom_edge_link(aes(edge_width = sim), alpha = 0.6, colour = "grey40") +
  geom_node_point(aes(colour = factor(suburb)), size = 3, alpha = 0.7) +
  scale_edge_width(range = c(0.2, 1), guide = "none") +
  scale_color_manual(values = whanganui_palette(10)) +  
  labs(title = "Similar location, similar QV.",
       subtitle = "Rateable units cluster within suburb streets, not between suburbs.",
       colour = "Suburb",
       caption = "network made with representative sample of 997 units.") +
  theme_void(base_family = "Inter") +
  theme(legend.position = "right",
        plot.title = element_text(size = 20),
        plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 15))

```

So, if there isn't a clear reason for rate differences accountable in the physical world, what may account for this behaviour? Rates are linked to QV valuations. QV valuations use sales data and consents (assumed improvement) calculate a home's value, which is used to adjust rates. What this means is that rates are, to some degree, influenced by how desirable a house is. If this were true, then considering what we know so far about suburb rates, then we would expect that houses closer together would have similar QV values (and hence rates) and that this would be represented within streets and suburbs. Which is what we see in the network plot below. Small clusters of units (points) of a single colour (suburb).

This accounts for why some suburbs pay more rates proportionally and why area isn't reflected in the median rates paid. More desirable areas pay more. Increased home value in one area passively raises nearby home values, leading to higher rates. This isn't 'fair'. It means that rate increases are effectively a premium paid for living in a house other people want to live in.

```{r graph 5 output, fig.width=8, fig.height= 4}
#|fig.width: 8
#|fig.height: 4

QV_cluster
```

So, who pays the most?\
The owner of unit 4849 is one answer.\
Residents of Otamatea is another.\
And whoever lives in the homes other people want to live in, is another answer.
